pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Common Plants & Trees

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 Plants):** "identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees." Naming real plants from observation, and sorting trees into deciduous (loses leaves) vs evergreen (keeps leaves), is statutory in England.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct naming PE; nearest anchor 1-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.A):** NGSS does not require naming particular plants; it frames plants by their external parts (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits) and their functions. The US connection here is recognising plants as organisms with parts, not the UK naming/deciduous–evergreen task.

- **Operational details:** This is primarily a NAMING-from-observation topic, best rooted in direct, first-hand encounters with real plants — a nature walk, the school grounds, a planted pot — rather than pictures alone, because the objective is that children recognise and name plants they actually meet. Build a shared vocabulary of five-plus common local plants (daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly...) and repeatedly name them in context. Introduce deciduous vs evergreen through the single observable test: does this tree drop all its leaves in autumn/winter, or stay green? Reinforce across seasons if possible (the same tree, bare then leafy). Keep 'plant' inclusive of trees — children often don't count a tree as a plant.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–6, KS1 Y1). Children can name at least five common plants from real specimens/pictures, match names to plants, and sort trees into deciduous and evergreen with examples. Appropriate: local, familiar species; the leaf-drop test. NOT appropriate yet: classification keys, Latin names, flower-part reproduction. Watch the 'a tree is not a plant' and 'evergreens never lose any leaves' misconceptions.
bestPractices: Root naming in first-hand observation of real, local plants (nature walk, school grounds, a grown pot) rather than pictures alone, since the objective is recognising plants children actually meet.
Build and rehearse a shared vocabulary of five-plus common local species, naming them repeatedly in context.
Teach deciduous vs evergreen through one observable test — does it drop all its leaves in autumn/winter or stay green — ideally by revisiting the same tree across seasons.
Explicitly include trees within the category 'plant' to counter the common belief that trees are not plants.
Use real specimens and picture cards together, and matching/sorting activities with self-checking feedback.
keyRepresentations: A named local-plant gallery (daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly) tied to real specimens.
Two sorting bins: deciduous (loses leaves) vs evergreen (keeps leaves), with tree examples.
Same-tree seasonal pair images (summer leafy / winter bare or still-green) to make the leaf-drop test visible.
Name–to–picture matching cards for common plants.
commonMisconceptions: 'A tree is not a plant' — children exclude large woody plants from the category 'plant'.
'Evergreen means it never loses a single leaf' — rather than keeping foliage year-round while shedding gradually.
Calling any small green plant 'grass' or 'weed' instead of using specific names.
Thinking deciduous trees are 'dead' in winter because they have no leaves.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year-olds learning to name common local plants and sort trees as deciduous (drops all its leaves in autumn/winter) or evergreen (stays leafy year-round, shedding only gradually). Learning is rooted in first-hand observation of real, local plants, supported by an illustrated tap-to-reveal scene that binds each plant to its name and one recognition cue, a season slider that makes the leaf-drop test visible on the same tree, and matching/sorting follow-up checks. Key misconceptions to pre-empt: a tree is not a plant, evergreens never shed any leaf, and a bare winter tree is dead.

activities.title: Nature walk: find, name and rehearse real local plants
feedback: If a child calls any small green plant 'grass' or 'weed', offer the specific name and have them repeat it in context.
If a child excludes a tree from 'plants', point out its roots, stem/trunk and leaves and confirm a tree is a plant too.
Praise naming tied to a feature ('yes — holly, because the leaves are shiny and spiky all year').
activities.rationale: The statutory objective is naming from first-hand observation, so direct encounters with real, local species build recognition rather than only testing it. Explicitly placing trees inside 'plant' counters a documented misconception.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
Children frequently do not classify trees as plants, and hold that 'evergreen' means a tree never loses any leaves — common primary botany misconceptions to pre-empt.
learnerActions: Go outside to the school grounds, a park, a nature walk, or a planted pot and look closely at real plants.
Find and name at least five common local plants (for example daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly), saying each name aloud as you find it.
Point to a recognition feature as you name each one — for example the dandelion's jagged leaves and clock seedhead, the holly's shiny spiky leaves.
Deliberately include a big tree (such as an oak) and say 'a tree IS a plant' to confirm trees belong in the plant group.

Over the seasons, especially from autumn into winter, return to the same tree to see whether it keeps its green leaves or goes bare (some young oaks and beech hedges hold dry brown leaves until spring, but they are still deciduous).
activities.intendedInsight: Plants (including trees) are organisms you can recognise and name from how they really look, and the names belong to plants you actually meet.

activities.title: Tap-to-explore seasonal park scene (indoor anchor)
feedback: When a tree is flipped bare, confirm 'deciduous — it drops all its leaves, then grows new ones in spring'.
When the evergreen stays green, confirm 'evergreen — it keeps leaves all year, though it does drop a few at a time'.
If a child says the bare tree is dead, show that new leaves grow back in the spring state.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored word–image mapping ties each plant to its name and distinguishing look, and showing the same tree in two seasonal states makes the single observable test (does it go bare?) visible. The scene also directly works against two documented misconceptions: tapping the oak among the plants confirms a tree is a plant, and the 'drops a few at a time' feedback counters the belief that an evergreen never loses any leaf. This indoor scene is a proposed scaffold to name and rehearse what the child then finds for real outdoors; it supplements rather than replaces the walk.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
Children frequently do not classify trees as plants, and hold that 'evergreen' means a tree never loses any leaves — common primary botany misconceptions to pre-empt.
learnerActions: Tap each plant in an illustrated park scene to see/hear its name plus one recognition cue (tap the dandelion to highlight its jagged leaves and clock seedhead; tap the daisy, buttercup, rose).
Tap a big oak included among the plants to confirm that a tree is a plant.

For each tree, open a lift-the-flap or slide a year-slider that swings the SAME tree from summer to winter: flip the oak and watch it go bare ('deciduous: drops its leaves'); flip the holly beside it and watch it stay glossy green ('evergreen: keeps its leaves').
Say whether each tree is deciduous or evergreen based on what you just saw happen.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciduous/evergreen rule is something you observe — a deciduous tree goes completely bare and regrows, an evergreen stays green all year (shedding only gradually) — not just a definition to memorise.

activities.title: Sort trees into two bins with a year that runs forward
feedback: If a sort is wrong, run the year forward so the leaf-drop (or not) is visible, then let the child re-sort.
If a child judges by how a tree looks on one day, remind them the rule is about the whole year, not a single snapshot.
activities.rationale: Sorting makes the defining leaf-drop test observable through a season control, while matching rehearses name recognition. The year-slider that drops and regrows leaves is the key interaction that makes the rule visible.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
learnerActions: Use two labelled bins: deciduous (loses leaves) and evergreen (keeps leaves).
Drag each tree into a bin, then run a season slider forward ('run the year forward') to check: a deciduous tree strips all its leaves while an evergreen stays green.
Pair this with a name-the-plant drag-match: drag each plant name onto the matching picture or real specimen.
Explain how you could tell which group a tree belongs to by watching it across a whole year.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciduous vs evergreen is decided across the whole year (does the tree go completely bare?), and each plant has a name you can match to its appearance.

activities.title: Check: match names and sort trees (follow-up assessment)
feedback: Full understanding: explains a deciduous tree drops all its leaves seasonally and regrows them (bare ≠ dead), an evergreen keeps leaves year-round, and transfers the rule to a new example such as a larch (a conifer that drops all its needles, so deciduous).
Partial: knows 'deciduous loses its leaves' as a fact but still leans on present appearance or thinks a bare tree has died — revisit the same-tree seasonal pair.
Gap: names trees only by how they look right now and calls a bare deciduous tree 'dead' — reteach with the four-season picture strip and the dormant-not-dead check.
activities.rationale: Matching and categorization assess the naming and sorting objectives directly. Because they check recognition rather than build it from observation, they belong after the observational and interactive work, as follow-up; recognition alone does not elicit the spoken naming or reasoning the objective also expects.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
learnerActions: Match five named plants to their pictures or real specimens.
Sort six trees into deciduous and evergreen, giving an example of each.
Answer the diagnostic: 'The oak is bare with no leaves in winter; the holly has green leaves all year. Which is deciduous — and how could you tell just by watching it across a whole year?'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner reasons from leaf loss over the year (the oak goes bare then regrows), not from how a tree looks on one day.

activities.title: Dormant-not-dead twig investigation (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: If a child predicts nothing will happen because the stick is dead, keep the twigs visible as the buds swell and open, then revisit the prediction; if a twig does not open, use the scratch test and a spring photo instead.
Confront the 'bare = dead' idea directly with a spring photo of the same tree in full leaf.
Clarify for evergreens: they do shed leaves, a few at a time and continuously replaced, so the tree is never completely bare — show fallen holly or pine leaves beneath an evergreen.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task is proposed to surface and challenge the 'bare tree is dead' misconception by letting children watch buds leaf out; observing real bud-burst may make the dormant-not-dead idea more concrete than a verbal statement, though its relative effectiveness is not established here.
learnerActions: In late winter, with permission, have an adult cut a few bare twigs from a deciduous tree (for example horse chestnut with sticky buds) and stand them in water on a windowsill.
Predict what the bare 'dead-looking stick' will do over the next few weeks, and say WHY.
Watch over the next two to four weeks as the buds usually swell and begin to open into small leaves (some twigs may not open).
Discuss: is a bare winter tree alive or dead, and how could you check (scratch a twig to show green underneath, point to waiting buds)?
activities.intendedInsight: A bare deciduous tree in winter is dormant, not dead — it still holds buds and will leaf again in spring.

constraints: Appropriate content: local, familiar species and the single leaf-drop test. NOT appropriate yet: classification keys, Latin names, and flower-part reproduction.
Keep 'plant' inclusive of trees throughout, since children often exclude large woody plants from the category.

The illustrated scene and sorting bins are indoor scaffolds that name and rehearse; they supplement but do not replace the first-hand outdoor observation the naming-from-observation objective requires.
Matching and sorting checks confirm recognition but do not by themselves build it from observation, nor elicit spoken naming; use them as follow-up, not as the main teaching.
Teach that evergreens DO shed leaves gradually (never going bare), rather than that they never lose a single leaf.

NGSS has no plant-naming performance expectation; its nearest anchor (1-LS1-1 / LS1.A) frames plants by external parts and functions, which is a different objective from the UK naming/deciduous–evergreen task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source row marks the two misconception/NGSS claims as verified:false and only the DfE claim as verified:true; sourceClaims reflect the claims as written and do not upgrade their evidence status.

The in-role conversation and manipulable 3D tree were judged poor fit in the source; omitted as activities rather than reproduced as categorical 'medium adds nothing' claims, since no distinct learning purpose was given.

The larch example (a conifer that drops all its needles) is used as a 'tricky case' for deciduous reasoning; keep it as an extension for learners who have secured the basic rule, not as an early example.

The 'bare winter tree is dead' misconception targeted by the twig investigation is drawn from the assessment error patterns in the original row, not from a cited sources[].claim; its activity sourceClaims are therefore [].
The twig investigation's efficacy relative to verbal correction is an untested proposal; efficacy wording is kept qualified.

assess.poeTask: In late winter, cut a few bare twigs from a deciduous tree (e.g. horse chestnut with sticky buds) and stand them in water on the windowsill. Ask each child to predict what the 'dead-looking stick' will do over two weeks and WHY. A child holding 'bare = dead' predicts nothing will happen; watching the buds burst and leaf out forces the dormant-not-dead idea.
probeDeeper: What will happen to the oak's leaves and branches in spring?
If I showed you both trees in July, when both are covered in leaves, how else could you work out which is deciduous?
Is the bare oak in winter alive or dead — how could you check?
A larch is a conifer with needles, but it drops every needle in winter — would you call it deciduous or evergreen, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The oak is deciduous because it drops all its leaves in autumn and grows new ones in spring; the holly is evergreen because it keeps leaves all year. The way to tell is to watch across the seasons for whether the tree goes completely bare.

errorPatterns.pattern: A bare tree in winter is dead ('the oak's got no leaves, it must have died')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish dormant from dead: scratch the twig to show green underneath, point to buds already waiting; it will leaf again in spring. Confront directly with a spring photo of the same tree.
errorPatterns.distractor: The oak is dead, not deciduous, because it has no leaves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the leafless winter oak 'dead' rather than deciduous, and is surprised it could grow leaves again

errorPatterns.pattern: Evergreens never drop a single leaf ('holly leaves stay on forever')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evergreens do shed leaves — a few at a time, replaced continuously — so the tree is never bare. Show fallen holly/pine leaves under an evergreen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists evergreen leaves never fall, so cannot explain how the tree replaces old leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the group by what the tree looks like right now, not across the year ('it has leaves today so it's evergreen')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Deciduous vs evergreen is about the whole year, not one day. Use a four-season picture strip of each tree.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In summer, when both trees are leafy, cannot tell them apart; relies on the present snapshot

responseLevels.gap: Names trees only from how they look at the moment; calls a bare deciduous tree 'dead'; cannot use the idea of losing leaves across the year.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a deciduous tree drops all its leaves seasonally and regrows them (bare ≠ dead), an evergreen keeps leaves year-round, and transfers the rule to a new example such as the larch.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 'deciduous loses its leaves' as a fact but still leans on the tree's present appearance, or thinks a bare tree has died, and cannot handle a tricky case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two trees. The oak is bare with no leaves in winter; the holly has green leaves all year round. Which one is deciduous — and how could you tell, just by watching it across a whole year?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept reasons from leaf loss over the year (the oak goes bare then regrows). A child who lacks it judges from the tree's state right now ("the oak has no leaves so it's dead / it's not a real tree") or picks an irrelevant cue like size, and cannot say what to watch for over time.
